turns.response_html: Friedrich Soennecken, a German entrepreneur, patented the first version of the hole puncher in 1886. However, Benjamin Smith patented an "improved" ticket punch in the U.S. in 1885, and Charles Brooks patented a paper punch in 1893.

Riveting dates back to Ancient Egypt, with evidence found in bronze tools and jewelry. While no single individual is credited with the invention, the modern blind rivet (pop rivet) was developed by Hamilton Neil Wylie in 1916 and later refined by the British United Shoe Machinery Company.

turns.prompt_text: why are rivets used over bolts
turns.response_html:
Rivets provide a permanent, vibration-resistant connection that is lighter and more aerodynamic than bolts. Because they expand to fill the hole, they distribute stress evenly, preventing the joint from loosening in high-strain environments like aircraft wings or bridge spans.

  • Permanent: Unlike bolts, they cannot vibrate loose over time.
  • Weight: Rivets are significantly lighter, which is critical for aerospace.
  • Tamper-Proof: They require destruction to remove, ensuring structural integrity.
  • Cost: Once automated, riveting is faster and cheaper for mass production.

While some heavy-duty steel rivets in construction were historically installed red-hot to shrink and tighten as they cooled, most modern applications rely on high-pressure compression to deform the metal and create a secure seal.

turns.prompt_text: Do all rivets require cold pressing
turns.response_html:
Not all rivets require cold pressing, though it is the most common method for modern, smaller-scale applications. The method used generally depends on the size of the rivet and the material of the structures being joined.

Here is a breakdown of the different installation processes:

1. Hot Riveting

Historically, this was the standard for massive steel structures like skyscrapers, bridges, and ships (including the Titanic).

  • The Process: Steel rivets were heated in a forge until they were glowing red-hot (roughly 500°C to 1,000°C).
  • The Benefit: Once hammered into place, the rivet would contract as it cooled. This thermal contraction pulled the metal plates together with incredible force, creating an extremely tight, leak-proof seal.

2. Cold Riveting (Cold Pressing)

This is the standard for aluminum and smaller steel rivets used in aerospace and general manufacturing.

  • The Process: The rivet is set at room temperature using high-pressure hydraulic presses or pneumatic "squeeze" tools.
  • The Benefit: It is faster, safer, and doesn't require a forge on-site. It is ideal for materials like aluminum, which could have their structural integrity compromised by extreme heat.

3. Specialty Methods

  • Blind (Pop) Riveting: These are set cold using a mandrel that is pulled through the rivet body until it snaps. No "pressing" of the head is required from the opposite side.
  • Self-Piercing Riveting: A high-speed cold process where the rivet is driven into the material without a pre-drilled hole, displacing the metal to create a mechanical interlock.

Summary Table

FeatureHot RivetingCold Riveting
Common MaterialsHeavy SteelAluminum, Thin Steel, Plastic
Primary ForceThermal ContractionMechanical Pressure
Historical UseBridges, Ships, BeamsAircraft, Appliances, Electronics
Seal QualitySuperior (due to shrinking)Excellent (due to hole expansion)

turns.response_html:
That extrusion you're seeing is likely the result of orbital riveting or radial riveting.

In high-quality consumer goods like a heavy-duty hole puncher, manufacturers often use these "cold forming" techniques to create a smooth, rounded head that acts as a permanent pivot. It creates that "extruded" look you mentioned without the mess of a hammer or the heat of a forge.

How it's done

Instead of hitting the rivet with one massive downward blow, a machine uses a rotating tool (called a peen) that moves in a specific path (circular or rosette-shaped).

  • The Process: The peen applies pressure at a slight angle—usually around 3° to 6°. As it rotates around the top of the pin, it "massages" or "rolls" the metal outward.
  • The Result: Only a small area of the metal is being deformed at any given millisecond. This requires much less force than traditional pressing and results in a very clean, uniform "extruded" lip.

Why use this for a hole puncher?

  1. Controlled Tension: Since the tool is computer-controlled, the manufacturer can stop the deformation at the exact micro-millimeter where the pieces are held together but can still rotate freely.
  2. No Stress Fractures: Because the metal is moved gently into its new shape, the pivot pin doesn't crack or become brittle, which is important for a tool you’ll be pressing down on thousands of times.
  3. Aesthetics: It leaves a smooth, professional finish that looks like part of the original rod, rather than a flattened "mushroom" head.

Fun Fact: If you look very closely at the extruded end with a magnifying glass, you might see very faint, concentric "swirl" marks left by the rotating tool!

turns.prompt_text: is it important for the metal to be hot or cold in this I imagine cold would be worse because you're not trying to form any bonds
turns.response_html:
Actually, using cold metal is usually preferred for this specific process. While it sounds counterintuitive, you aren't trying to melt the pieces together; you are performing mechanical fastening, not welding.

Why Cold is Better

  • Structural Integrity: Heating metal can change its internal grain structure, often making it softer or more brittle. Cold forming actually work-hardens the rivet, making the pivot point stronger and more wear-resistant over time.
  • Precision Fit: Hot metal shrinks as it cools. If you used heat on a hole puncher pivot, the rivet might shrink too much, creating a "wobbly" joint. Cold forming allows the manufacturer to expand the metal to the exact diameter of the hole for a perfect, zero-clearance fit.
  • Material Compatibility: Many hole punchers use plated steel or aluminum. High heat would destroy the finish or melt the lighter components, whereas cold orbital riveting preserves the surface aesthetics.

In this context, the "bond" isn't a chemical or thermal one—it is a physical interference fit where the metal is simply moved into a shape that can no longer pass back through the hole.

turns.prompt_text: Is there any way to create a rivet like this at home
turns.response_html:
Creating an orbital rivet at home is difficult because it requires a specialized machine to "knead" the metal, but you can achieve a very similar, professional-looking permanent pivot using a technique called peening.

Here is how you can create a smooth, "extruded" looking rivet at home using basic tools:

1. The "Hammer and Anvil" Method (Manual Peening)

To get that flared-out look without a machine, you use a series of light, angled taps rather than one heavy blow.

  • Materials: A soft steel or brass rod (dowel) that fits your hole.
  • The Setup: Cut the rod so it sticks out only about 1.5mm to 2mm on each side. If it's too long, it will bend; if it's too short, it won't flare.
  • The Technique:
    1. Place one end of the rod on a hard steel surface (an anvil or the back of a vise).
    2. Use the ball-peen side of a hammer (the rounded end).
    3. Tap the edges of the rod at an angle, moving in a circle. You are "rolling" the edge of the metal down, just like the orbital machine does.
    4. Flip the piece over and repeat on the other side.

2. The "Drill Press" Hack (Pseudo-Orbital)

If you have a drill press, you can simulate the "rolling" action to get a much smoother finish than a hammer.

  • The Tool: You can buy or grind a rivet spinning tool (a hardened steel bit with a concave, polished "cup" at the end).
  • The Process: 1. Secure your project so it cannot move. 2. Put the spinning tool in the drill press. 3. Turn the press to a medium speed. 4. Lower the spinning tool onto the rod with steady pressure. The friction and rotation will "burnish" and flare the metal outward into a perfectly round, shiny head.

3. Using a "Center Punch"

If you want that "extruded" look specifically (where the center looks slightly hollowed or pressed in):

  1. Use a center punch (the pointy tool used for marking metal).
  2. Place the point in the dead center of your rod end.
  3. Strike it firmly. This forces the metal from the center outward toward the edges, creating a flared rim.
  4. Follow up with a flat hammer to smooth the rim down.

Key Tips for Home Success:

  • Anneal the metal: If you are using a tough steel rod, heat it with a torch until it's red and let it cool slowly before you start. This makes the metal "dead soft" and much easier to flare while cold.
  • Support is everything: The rod must be supported on a completely solid surface. Any "bounce" in your setup will cause the rivet to fail or look messy.
  • Don't over-tighten: If this is a pivot (like your hole puncher), place a thin piece of paper between the moving parts before you rivet. Once you're done, pull the paper out—this leaves just enough "play" for the parts to move.
